t: Club Garibaldi opens: an Italian mutual aid society's corner club, 1943
d: In 1943 Bay View's Garibaldi Lodge turned an old corner tavern at Russell and Superior into Club Garibaldi, with orchestra dancing every Friday and Saturday.

t: Lance Sijan: the Bay View High standout who received the Medal of Honor
d: In November 1967, Air Force Capt. Lance Sijan, a Bay View High graduate, was shot down over Laos. His courage as a prisoner earned him the Medal of Honor.

t: DeMarinis: Bay View's pizza family since 1949
d: In 1949 Vincent and Lucille DeMarinis opened a tavern at Wentworth and Potter. Within two years it was an Italian kitchen, and the DeMarinis name still means pizza in Bay View.

t: Armistice week, 1918: 10,000 Bay View marchers fill Humboldt Park
d: In November 1918, days after the armistice, more than 10,000 Bay View residents marched down KK and Logan to Humboldt Park to honor the neighborhood's soldiers.

t: The Llewellyn Library: Bay View's hilltop branch on Russell Avenue
d: In 1914, Bay View got its first purpose-built library: the Henry Llewellyn Branch on Russell Avenue, on land donated by Llewellyn's sons. It served the neighborhood until 1993.

t: The Hoan Bridge: Bay View's 'Bridge to Nowhere'
d: Built in the early 1970s, the Hoan Bridge sat finished but unconnected for years, mocked as the 'Bridge to Nowhere,' before it finally opened to traffic in 1977.

t: Three Brothers: the Schlitz saloon that became a Serbian landmark
d: In 1897 Schlitz built a turreted tavern on St. Clair Street. Six decades later a Serbian family turned it into Three Brothers, still serving today.

t: Beulah Brinton, the mill town's teacher, librarian and neighbor
d: In 1872, Beulah Brinton moved into a new house on Superior Street and opened it to the rolling mill's immigrant families. Her lending library grew into Milwaukee's first branch library.

t: Puddler's Hall, the iron workers' union hall that became a tavern
d: In the early 1870s, Bay View's iron puddlers built a union hall on St. Clair Street. More than 150 years later, Puddler's Hall is still pouring.

t: Kneisler's White House, Bay View's tavern "Capitol"
d: In the early 1890s, William Kneisler opened a turreted tavern at KK and Ellen. For a century, Kneisler's White House was where Bay View talked politics.

t: St. Augustine's steeple rises over Howell Avenue
d: In November 1908, Bay View's German Catholics dedicated St. Augustine of Hippo Church on Howell Avenue, the Brust & Philipp landmark still standing 118 years later.

t: The Avalon's comeback: Bay View gets its movie palace back
d: In November 2014, after 14 dark years and a $2.5 million restoration, the 1929 Avalon Theater on KK announced its reopening. It's still showing movies today.

t: Groppi's: the 1913 Italian grocery that got a second life
d: In November 2003, months after the last Groppi closed it, the 90-year-old Italian grocery at Russell and Wentworth reopened under new owners. It's still there.

t: Bay View governed itself as a village for eight years before its roughly 4,000 residents v…
d: Bay View governed itself as a village for eight years before its roughly 4,000 residents voted in 1887 to join Milwaukee, becoming the city's 17th Ward. The trade gave up independence for city services residents wanted, such as sewers, sidewalks and street lights. The Beulah Brinton House, pictured, was an early gathering place for the village and is now home to the Bay View Historical Society.

t: The North Chicago Rolling Mill (the iron works Bay View grew up around) as it looked in 18…
d: The North Chicago Rolling Mill (the iron works Bay View grew up around) as it looked in 1882. The village of Bay View had incorporated three years earlier with 2,592 people as Milwaukee's first suburb, and residents voted to join the city in 1887.
